clue.text: Everyman adhering to decency: that's surprising

definitions.note: The answer is an exclamation and the definition a remark about one, so the setter is naming what the phrase conveys rather than offering a word you could swap straight in.

indicators.note: To adhere to something is to stick fast against it, so this piece is glued on to the end of the word beside it rather than tucked inside it.

parts.note: Decency is the abstract moral quality — the noun for what a decent person has.
Everyman is the pen name of the Observer's setter, so the clue is pointing at whoever wrote it.

explanation.surface: The setter sticking to the proprieties, which apparently comes as a shock.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman signs the Observer's puzzle every week, so a clue naming him is naming its own author — and setters write themselves in as ME.
explanation.definitionFit: It is what people blurt out when something takes them aback, so the definition names the reaction the phrase exists to express.

clue.text: Runs away from bugs in stones

indicators.note: away from says the letter is taken out of the following word

parts.note: germs are bugs, as in a stomach bug
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Someone flees from insects hiding among rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugs' suggests insects, but it means germs; taking R 'away from' GERMS leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Gems are precious stones, such as rubies or diamonds.

clue.text: 'Hey you, getting nookie regularly?' — swinish outburst

indicators.note: getting says the first piece acquires the second, joined after it

parts.note: oi is a British shout to get someone's attention

indicators.note: regularly here means every third letter, starting with the first

parts.note: the first and fourth letters of nookie are N and K

explanation.surface: Someone is rudely asked whether their love life is a regular thing.
explanation.walkthrough: OI 'getting' nookie taken 'regularly', every third letter, which gives NK. Nookie is slang for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: A pig's grunt is the sound a swine makes, so it is a piggy exclamation.

clue.text: Even pair of cheeks?

parts.note: Cheek in the British sense of brazen nerve — 'what a cheek!' — has a one-syllable slang twin, and that is what these letters spell.
A pair is two of the same thing, and the little word that joins two of anything stands between them.
The plural is asking for that same slang word a second time.

explanation.surface: A well-matched pair of buttocks.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheek meaning nerve is the sense in play — 'he had the neck to ask' — not the face or the backside the surface is pointing at.
explanation.definitionFit: Two horses running neck and neck are exactly level, so 'even' is the racing sense of dead level rather than anything to do with numbers.

clue.text: Sportsperson, senior, astride pedalled vehicle

indicators.note: Sitting astride something means having a leg on either side of it, so the short piece ends up split around the longer one.

parts.note: Sr is the tag added to a father's name to tell him apart from a son called the same thing.
A trike is a tricycle, pedalled like a bicycle but on three wheels.

explanation.surface: An elderly athlete perched on a tricycle.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing points at football until the first word, and 'sportsperson' is deliberately vague — the surface would much rather you pictured a veteran cyclist.
explanation.definitionFit: A striker is the forward whose job is scoring goals in football, so 'sportsperson' defines by category, one kind of player standing for the whole.

clue.text: The writer, politician: that man's ruined city

parts.note: The writer of a clue is its setter, and a setter writes themselves in with this two-letter word.
MP is a Member of Parliament, the standard British shorthand for a politician.
What belongs to that man is his.

explanation.surface: A writer and a politician standing about in some other man's wrecked city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruined' is the trap: it looks like an instruction to shuffle letters, and it is part of the definition, since the Egyptian city has been ruins for centuries.
explanation.definitionFit: Memphis, the capital of ancient Egypt, survives only as ruins south of Cairo, so the definition names it by the state it is in.

clue.text: Jazz fans with bit of sax moved to intro? Improvise lyrics

indicators.text: with bit of sax moved to intro
indicators.note: the bit of sax is its S, and moving it to the intro puts that letter at the start of the word

parts.note: cats is jazz slang for fans and players

explanation.surface: Jazz lovers want a sax phrase at the opening, then make up words.
explanation.walkthrough: In CATS, 'with bit of sax moved to intro' takes the S at the end round to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Scat singing replaces words with improvised nonsense syllables in jazz.

clue.text: After reshuffle, actualises hospital wards

indicators.note: A reshuffle deals the same cards out into new places, so the word beside it keeps its letters and loses their order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A shake-up that finally makes the hospital's wards happen.
explanation.walkthrough: Casualty is what British hospitals call A&E, the department the ambulances pull up at, and 'wards' in the plural is the setter's extension of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Casualty is the British hospital's emergency department, where ambulances bring the injured, so the plural names those wards.

clue.text: Short stick in play might effect these?

definitions.text: Short stick in play might effect these?

indicators.note: A ball in play is loose and being knocked about, so the letters beside it will not stay in the order they are printed.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A snooker player reaching for the short rest cue halfway through a frame.
explanation.walkthrough: The same two words are the picture and the fodder: the sentence describes what a cue can do while its opening words spell out the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight it describes them: a cue is the stick, and the fancy pots a player brings off with an awkward short one are what 'these' names.

clue.text: Hero — common ground — it's all black-and-white

indicators.note: Coffee is ground down to powder, and letters given that treatment can be swept back together in any order at all.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A hero, some common ground, and a situation with no grey areas anywhere in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Common ground' is such a natural pair that splitting it takes some doing — the second word is the instruction, not half of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A monochrome image is made in a single colour — in practice black, white and the greys between — which is what the phrase names in everyday speech.

clue.text: Sparkling wine in course of Lammas-tide

indicators.note: Whatever happens in the course of something happens inside it, so the letters wanted lie within the word that follows.

parts.note: Four consecutive letters, starting in the middle of the word and running straight across its hyphen.

explanation.surface: A glass of fizz drunk during the harvest festival.
explanation.walkthrough: Lammas is the old English harvest festival on 1 August and Lammas-tide the season around it; the word is here only for the letters it carries.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti is the sparkling white from the Piedmont town of the same name — Asti Spumante on the label — so the definition names it by type.

clue.text: In the main, disembark?

definitions.meaning: The reading the surface pushes is the everyday one — 'mostly', 'on the whole'.
The setter's reading is the pirate one: leaving the ship at cutlass point, with 'the main' as the open sea.

explanation.surface: A general remark about the business of getting off a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is an old word for the open sea — the Spanish Main — which is what turns a mild qualifier into a location.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking the plank is how a pirate crew made a prisoner leave the ship, so 'disembark' is the polite word for a forced exit over the side.

clue.text: Those drawn to light?

parts.note: The surface picture is moths circling a lamp — creatures that cannot help heading for a bulb.; Taken the setter's way the pull is towards lighting things, and 'drawn' shifts from being attracted to being compelled.

explanation.surface: Moths circling a lamp on a summer night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' reads as a noun the whole way through the clue and is a verb — the one word that has to change job before the answer appears.
explanation.definitionFit: A pyromaniac has an uncontrollable urge to set fires, so the phrase only works once 'light' is read as the verb, meaning to set alight.

clue.text: My bulletin edited to provide name of English actress

indicators.note: An edited text has been cut about and reordered, so the words named give up their letters but not their arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A journalist's own news report going under a sub-editor's pencil.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hides the join by making 'edited' sound like part of the newsroom story rather than the instruction it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Emily Blunt is the English actor of The Devil Wears Prada and A Quiet Place, so what the answer supplies is exactly what the definition asks for: her name.

clue.text: Tactician gets artist in a lather

indicators.note: Something worked into a lather has been whipped up and churned about, so the letters just named come out thoroughly disturbed.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A planner working an artist up into a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets' looks like a link word joining the tactician to the artist, and it is fodder — that misdirection is what costs solvers the letter count.
explanation.definitionFit: A strategist plans the whole campaign; 'tactician' is the loose everyday synonym for the same planning mind, though tactics are strictly the smaller moves inside it.

clue.text: Adjusting to drama, I'm a fighter

indicators.note: Adjusting something shifts its parts into new positions, which is exactly what happens to the two words after it.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: An actor settling into a play and declaring himself a scrapper.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue speaks in the answer's own voice — 'I'm a fighter' — which is why the definition arrives sounding like a boast.
explanation.definitionFit: A matador is the bullfighter who faces the bull and makes the kill, so 'fighter' names him by his trade rather than by his temperament.

clue.text: Type of jeans — covering expanse?

definitions.meaning: The denim sold with elastane in it takes this word in front of its name.
A long unbroken run of road, water or open country goes by the same word.

explanation.surface: A pair of jeans roomy enough to cover a lot of ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covering' does nothing but join the two senses, and it is what makes the clue read as a single thought about oversized denim.
explanation.definitionFit: Stretch jeans are the ones woven with elastane so they give, and a stretch of road or water is an expanse of it: the give and the extent.

clue.text: Bucolic site, comfy home, minimal in extremis …

parts.note: A lea is a meadow, the poets' word for open pasture.
A nest is the snuggest home a bird could ask for.

explanation.surface: An estate agent's advert for a snug country place with nothing surplus in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In extremis' looks like the standard instruction to take a word's outer letters, and it does no such thing: it belongs to the definition, pushing 'minimal' to its limit.
explanation.definitionFit: The leanest of anything has had every spare ounce taken off it, which is what 'minimal' pushed to its limit describes.

clue.text: Per Spooner, that woman recorded description of a certain road junction

definitions.text: description of a certain road junction

indicators.note: per Spooner says the opening sounds of two words are swapped, as the Reverend Spooner was said to do

parts.note: she is the pronoun for that woman, said aloud as 'shee', which is the sound that gets swapped
taped means recorded

explanation.surface: As the Reverend Spooner put it, a woman taped an account of a crossroads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Per Spooner', 'shee taped' with the opening sounds swapped becomes 'tee shaped', and the tee sound is written simply as the letter T.
explanation.definitionFit: A T-shaped junction is one where a side road meets a main road at right angles, like the letter.

clue.text: … extremely stinky component of amalgam — i.e., stinkiest

indicators.note: A component sits inside the thing it belongs to, so what is wanted is a run of letters lying within the words that follow.

parts.note: Seven consecutive letters starting inside the first word, running through the two-letter abbreviation and on into the last.

explanation.surface: The part of a mixture that reeks worse than anything else in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash and the full stops make the letters look separated when they run straight on, and 'i.e.' does surface duty while lending two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamy meat has hung long enough to smell high, so the superlative is the strongest-smelling of a set and 'extremely' carries the -est.

clue.text: Primarily, God's archangel bringing reports (I.eleven, Luke)?

definitions.text: Primarily, God's archangel bringing reports (I.eleven, Luke)?

indicators.note: primarily means taking the first letter of each word

parts.note: the first letters of these four words are G, A, B and R
the first letters of I, eleven and Luke are I, E and L

explanation.surface: A Bible reference: chapter one, verse eleven of Luke, where God's messenger brings news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primarily' takes the first letters: GABR from the first four words, then IEL. The whole clue describes him: in Luke 1:11 an angel appears to Zacharias, later naming himself as this archangel.
explanation.definitionFit: Gabriel is the archangel who brings God's messages in the Gospel of Luke, announcing two births.

clue.text: As a flooded river may come at too high a price

definitions.meaning: Taken literally, going over the top is what a river in spate does to its edges.

definitions.text: come at too high a price
definitions.meaning: The idiom for costing more than anybody can afford, where the bank is the one that holds money.

explanation.surface: A river in spate and the bill for the damage it leaves behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase started at the gaming table, where a player wins more than the house has set aside to pay out; the flood is the older, more literal picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of bank in one phrase: the river's edge a flood bursts through, and the store of money an expense empties.

clue.text: Upon rising, give out prison sentence

indicators.note: A down entry read upwards runs from the bottom of the grid to the top, so a word said to be rising arrives back to front.

parts.note: To give out heat, light or a smell is to emit it.

explanation.surface: A judge who gets out of bed and hands down a jail term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give out' looks as though it belongs with the sentencing, since giving out sentences is what courts do, and it is the wordplay instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing time is serving a prison sentence, and the word carries that sense on its own once a judge has handed one down.

clue.text: Money posted (we're told)

indicators.note: Being told something means hearing it, so the word wanted is one that sounds the same rather than one that looks the same.

parts.note: Something posted has been sent, and that word said aloud is written the coin's way.

explanation.surface: Cash that has gone off in the post, by all accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is hidden or shuffled here: the whole device is hearing the postal word instead of reading it, in a clue three words long.
explanation.definitionFit: A cent is the hundredth part of a dollar or a euro, so 'money' defines by example: one small coin standing in for the category.

clue.text: Military subdivision incapable: France lost

indicators.note: lost says the letter for France disappears from the word

parts.note: unfit means not capable
F is the international vehicle code for France

explanation.surface: An army division is useless after France was defeated.
explanation.walkthrough: With F 'lost' from UNFIT, the answer remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a subdivision of an army, such as a battalion or company.

clue.text: Maximally improve A.I. — almost too simple, dubiously

indicators.note: dubiously says the letters are arranged in a doubtful, unreliable order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters A and I

indicators.note: almost means the word loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Using artificial intelligence to perfect things is perhaps too easy, a sceptic says.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts TOO to TO; 'dubiously' then rearranges A, I, TO and SIMPLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To optimise or optimalise something is to make it as good as possible.

clue.text: Flipping American junk: I'm off

indicators.note: Flipping something turns it over end for end, so the two pieces once assembled are read the other way round.

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for American.
Tat is British for cheap rubbish — the stuff on a jumble-sale table.

explanation.surface: Dumping some cheap American rubbish and walking out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' is a mild British swear word in the surface, where it seems to be insulting the junk rather than turning anything round.
explanation.definitionFit: Ta-ta is the British goodbye, nursery and pub alike, so 'I'm off' is what somebody is saying at the moment they use it.

clue.text: Youngster's amateur haircut with, after vacation, loathsome cologne

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for amateur, as on an amateur golfer's entry.
A do is a hairdo, what you come out of the salon with.

indicators.note: A vacated word has had its insides emptied out, leaving only the letters standing at either end.

parts.note: Emptied out, the word is left with only the letters at its two ends.
Cologne is a scent, and the lower-case c says the perfume rather than the city.

explanation.surface: A kid with a home-done haircut and a bottle of horrible aftershave.
explanation.walkthrough: Cologne keeps a lower-case c because it is the perfume, not the German city that gave the perfume its name — a capital would have given the game away.
explanation.definitionFit: An adolescent is somebody in their teens, between child and adult, so 'youngster' is the everyday word for the same person.
